To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the inclusion of dietary n-3 fatty acids in ruminant diets increased the n-3 fatty acid content in the meat.

(i) the n-3 fatty acids in meat are increased by feeding diets with high levels of n-3 fatty acid, (ii) the n-6/n3 fatty acid ratio is decreased, (iii) the n-9 and n-7 fatty acids are increased in parallel, (iv) the P/S ratio is not changed, (v) the c9t11-CLA content in ruminant meat is not increased, and (vi) the CLA content in
the n-3 fatty acid content of meat can be improved by feeding fish oil or forage to ruminants, and that the CLA content of meat can only be increased by feeding CLA-rich oils to monogastrics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of new technologies and strategies for the improvement of the nutritional value and quality of animal products.
the effect of feeding ruminant and monogastric animals diets rich in polyunsaturated fatty and/or CLA isomers on the incorporation of these fatty acids in the intramusular fat of meat.
the effects of dietary fatty acids, especially n-3 and LA on the deposition of these fatty acids in meat of beef, lamb, pork, and chicken.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

increasing the n-3 and CLA content in animal meats is possible but not always easy and that the effect of nutritional factors on the fatty acid profile is dependent on animal species and the fatty acid of interest.

feeding n-3 rich (LNA, fish oil/fish meals) or high concentrate diets (rich in LA) to ruminants resulted in an increased content of n-3 fatty acids, in particular the long chain n-3 fatty acid DHA, in meat.
increasing n-3 content of meat is possible but not always achieved, and increasing CLA content in ruminant meats is not always successful.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the intramuscular fatty acid composition of beef, lamb or pork meat can be manipulated by dietary fatty acids, however, the effect on intramusular fatty acid composition is species dependent and the response of the animals to dietary fatty acids is highly variable.

the n-3 fatty acid content in the meat is mainly determined by the n-3 dietary fatty acid supply, while the CLA content in the meat of monogastric animals is mainly determined by including CLA-rich oils in the diet.

the incorporation of long chain fatty acids and CLA in meat can be increased by dietary manipulation of fatty acid composition, however the magnitude of the increase depends on the animal species and fatty acid.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the intramuscular fatty acid composition of beef, lamb, and pork can be manipulated by dietary means.
increasing the n-3 and CLA content in meat of ruminants can be accomplished by dietary means, but that the effects are rather modest.
the n-3 long chain content in the intracellular fat of beef and lamb is increased by including fish oil in the diet.
